content.title: About
content.content: Chitterlings are boiled or fried intestines (most commonly pork) that are a traditional dish in Southern US, Eastern European, and Asian cuisines. They have a strong aroma, a dense meaty texture, and are often served with spicy sauces or as a side dish.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The word “chitterlings” derives from an old English term meaning “small things.”
In the United States they are traditionally prepared for Thanksgiving and New Year celebrations.
In some regions they are considered a delicacy, while in others they are known as “poor‑man's food.”
They can be cooked in many ways: boiled, fried, baked, or marinated.
In Japan a similar dish called “moto‑no‑ko” is often served with teriyaki sauce.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Chitterlings provide about 20 g of protein per 100 g, making them a good protein source.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: They contain vitamin B12, niacin, and riboflavin, which support energy metabolism.

items.title: Contains minerals
items.content: Chitterlings are a source of iron, zinc, and selenium, nutrients important for immunity and blood formation.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: They fit well into low‑carb diets for those monitoring carbohydrate intake.

items.title: Food‑borne illness risk
items.content: Intestines can harbor harmful bacteria (Salmonella, E. coli). Thorough cooking is essential.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to animal meat.

items.title: High cholesterol
items.content: Chitterlings contain a notable amount of cholesterol, so people with hypercholesterolemia should limit consumption.

items.title: Preparation challenges
items.content: Improper cleaning can leave bile residues, resulting in a bitter taste.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Chitterlings are usually boiled until tender, then fried with onion, garlic, and spices. They can be served as a snack, added to stews, soups, or used as a filling for pies.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh chitterlings in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C for no more than 2 days. Frozen portions last up to 3 months in an airtight bag. Before cooking, rinse thoroughly and trim excess fat.
